findings.title: Memory Pressure and OOM History
findings.explanation:
Over the last 10 / 60 / 300 seconds, at least one program was stalled waiting for memory 0.0% / 0.0% / 0.0% of the time, and all programs were stalled at once 0.0% / 0.0% / 0.0% of the time.

No meaningful stalls at the moment: programs are getting the memory they ask for without waiting.

The kernel has killed 1 process since boot because memory ran out. This counts both a whole machine out of RAM and a program or service exceeding its own memory limit (a container or systemd MemoryMax).
findings.recommendation:
1. Confirm what is happening now (the pressure file should be near zero on a healthy machine; in vmstat, non-zero si/so columns mean active swapping):
    cat /proc/pressure/memory
    vmstat 1 5
2. Find out who was killed and why (the log says whether the whole machine or a single memory limit was the cause):
    sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'out of memory|oom-kill|killed process'
3. Reduce the demand: qemu-system-x86 holds the most private memory (96.6 GB). The Used memory page lists the consumers and what to do about each.
4. There is no swap, so the kernel has nothing to relieve the pressure with. The Swap configuration finding has the zram and swap file commands.
5. Stop one runaway service from taking the whole machine down by giving it a ceiling (MemoryHigh slows it first, MemoryMax is the hard limit), and shield the services that must survive with a negative OOM score:
    sudo systemctl set-property <service> MemoryHigh=<N>G MemoryMax=<M>G
    sudo systemctl edit <critical-service>     # add: [Service] OOMScoreAdjust=-900
6. Let a userspace daemon act early, while the machine is still responsive, instead of waiting for the kernel's OOM killer. systemd-oomd needs systemd 248+ and cgroup v2; earlyoom is the alternative that works anywhere:
    sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-oomd
    sudo apt install earlyoom && sudo systemctl enable --now earlyoom

findings.title: Memory Usage Overview
findings.explanation:
Of 247.5 GB of RAM, 159.4 GB (64.4%) is in use by programs and the kernel, and 88.1 GB (35.6%) is available for new allocations without swapping — comfortable. These are the 'used' and 'available' columns of free(1).

Only 18.1 GB is completely unused, and that is normal: Linux fills spare RAM with cache and hands it back the moment a program asks. free(1) shows 72.1 GB as 'buff/cache', but that figure includes 433 MB of shared memory (tmpfs, /dev/shm, graphics buffers) which stays in RAM; the part the kernel can genuinely give back is 71.7 GB.

What matters is 'available', not 'free'. The Used memory, Page cache, Shared memory, Swap, Pressure and Kernel tuning pages break this number down.

findings.title: Page Cache
findings.explanation:
The page cache holds 67.1 GB (27.1% of RAM): copies of files recently read or written, kept so the next access is served from memory instead of the disk. Disk-block buffers add 1.4 GB.

63.0 GB of the file cache has not been touched recently (the kernel drops that first) and 5.5 GB is in active use. Running programs map 2.2 GB of it.

Reclaimable kernel caches (the dentry and inode caches that remember file names and metadata) add 3.1 GB.

This memory is not wasted: it makes file access fast and is handed back to programs the moment they ask for it.

A large cache is therefore a sign of a healthy machine, not a leak. Emptying it (echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) frees nothing of lasting value: it only forces files to be read from the disk again and slows everything down until the cache is rebuilt. It is a benchmarking tool, not an optimisation.

ZFS keeps its own cache (the ARC) outside the page cache; it is described under Kernel memory.

findings.title: Dirty Page / Writeback Pressure
findings.explanation:
2 MB is waiting to be written to disk (0.0% of what can be dirtied), comfortably below the background threshold of 8.7 GB.

Background writeback starts at 8.7 GB and writers are slowed from 13.0 GB; the hard limit is 17.3 GB. These are measured against 86.6 GB (free memory plus file cache).

On this machine the ratio settings allow up to 17.3 GB of dirty data to pile up before writers are blocked. Flushing that much at once can freeze programs for many seconds on a slow disk; many administrators cap it with fixed byte limits instead.
findings.recommendation:
1. Optional: cap the amount of dirty data with fixed limits (256 MB to start background writeback, 1 GB before writers block). Setting the byte values replaces the ratios:
    sudo sysctl vm.dirty_background_bytes=268435456 vm.dirty_bytes=1073741824
    printf 'vm.dirty_background_bytes = 268435456\nvm.dirty_bytes = 1073741824\n' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-dirty.conf

findings.explanation:

Where it lives — tmpfs mounts (files that exist only in RAM):

  2. /run/user/1000 — 16 MB of 24.8 GB (0.1% full)

findings.title: Kernel Swappiness Setting
findings.explanation:
vm.swappiness is 100 (kernel default 60). It decides how eagerly the kernel moves idle program memory to swap instead of dropping file cache: low values protect programs' memory, high values protect the file cache. The scale runs from 0 to 200.

No swap is configured, so there is nowhere to move program memory and this setting has no effect on it. See Swap configuration.

findings.title: Swap Configuration
findings.explanation:
Swap: none configured.

No swap is configured. Without it the kernel can only reclaim file cache; once that is gone, the only option left is the OOM killer. Even a small swap lets idle program memory move out of the way and gives a memory spike somewhere to go. (Exceptions: Kubernetes nodes, where the kubelet expects swap off by default, and appliances that deliberately prefer an OOM kill to slowness.)
findings.recommendation:
1. Preferred: compressed RAM swap (zram). It needs no disk space, causes no disk wear and is much faster than swap on a disk. This sets it to half of RAM, kept after reboot:
    sudo apt install systemd-zram-generator     # Fedora, Arch, openSUSE: zram-generator
    printf '[zram0]\nzram-size = ram / 2\ncompression-algorithm = zstd\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
    sudo systemctl start systemd-zram-setup@zram0.service
2. Or a swap file of 8 GB on disk (ext4 or xfs; on Btrfs use 'btrfs filesystem mkswapfile' instead of fallocate):
    sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile
    sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
    sudo mkswap /swapfile
    sudo swapon /swapfile
    echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab   # keep it after reboot

findings.title: Kernel Memory
findings.explanation:
The kernel itself holds 6.0 GB of RAM (2.4%): 5.5 GB of slab caches (3.1 GB reclaimable, 2.3 GB not), 348 MB of page tables, 48 MB of kernel stacks and 142 MB of per-CPU data. This memory belongs to no program; it is the cost of running the system.

ZFS is loaded. Its cache (the ARC) holds 41.0 GB (16.5% of RAM, limit 246.5 GB). ZFS allocates it itself, outside the page cache, and /proc/meminfo's 'available' figure does not count it — so a ZFS machine always looks fuller than it is. ZFS does give the memory back when programs ask, but more slowly than the page cache does.

vm.min_free_kbytes is 88 MB: the reserve the kernel keeps free so it can always satisfy urgent allocations.

96.6 GB of RAM (39.0%) is locked and can never be swapped or reclaimed (mlock, ramfs, memory held by some drivers). 96.6 GB of it is locked by programs with mlock.

findings.title: Memory Overcommit Policy
findings.explanation: Overcommit is in heuristic mode (the default): the kernel lets programs reserve more memory than exists and refuses only absurd single requests. Programs have reserved 126.0 GB of address space (50.9% of RAM). A reservation is a promise, not use: big runtimes (Java, Go, browsers) and fork() reserve far more than they touch.

findings.title: Huge Pages
findings.explanation: Transparent huge pages are set to 'madvise': only programs that explicitly ask for huge pages get them. This is the safe middle ground and what most distributions recommend for servers. Right now 96.0 GB of program memory sits on huge pages.

findings.title: Interface Errors/Drops — enp6s0
findings.explanation: enp6s0: RX errors 0.00%, RX drops 6.19%, TX errors 0.00%, TX drops 0.00% of packets. Sustained rates like this commonly point to a cabling, driver, duplex-mismatch, or switch-port problem rather than normal network conditions. This interface has 3 active SR-IOV VFs — on some NIC/driver combinations, traffic steered to a VF's own queue is counted in the physical function's rx_dropped without indicating a real link problem, so this number is less conclusive here than it would be without VFs. Check the VF interfaces' own stats (`ip -s link show <vf-iface>`) to see whether their traffic volume lines up with the drops.
findings.recommendation: Compare against the VF interfaces' own traffic (`ip -s link show <vf-iface>`) before assuming a cabling/driver problem — with SR-IOV active, elevated PF rx_dropped is often explained by VF-steered traffic rather than a real link issue. If the VF traffic doesn't account for it, then check `ethtool <iface>` and the cable/switch port as usual.

findings.title: Security Overview
evidence: 33 reachable from the network, 8 local only
none detected (rules not readable without root)
findings.explanation:
1 finding(s) need attention, worst first:

  [WARNING] No Firewall Detected

Every check is read-only. A security audit shows what is configured and what is reachable from here; it cannot see the router, the cloud security group or the network policy in front of the machine.

LinuxDoctor is running without root, so some things were out of sight: which program owns other users' sockets, the firewall rules themselves, password hashes in /etc/shadow and AppArmor's profile list. Run it with sudo for the complete picture; the checks that could not run say so in their own finding.

findings.title: No Firewall Detected
findings.explanation:
No firewall service (firewalld, ufw) is running. The rules themselves cannot be read without root, so a rule set loaded by hand would not be seen; run LinuxDoctor with sudo to be certain.

19 TCP service(s) other than SSH accept connections from the network (port(s) 53, 80, 111, 139, 445, 2049, 10000, 20000, 32400, 33741, 34191, 36533, 43753, 44575, 45339, 47129, 54095, 54751, 60243) with nothing in front of them on this machine. If the machine sits behind a router or a cloud provider's security group that already filters traffic, the risk is lower; a firewall on the machine itself is still the protection that follows it from one network to another, and that stops a program installed tomorrow from being exposed by surprise.
findings.recommendation:
1. Install ufw if it is not installed:
    sudo apt install ufw
2. Allow what must stay reachable before turning it on. These other TCP ports are open now: 53, 80, 111, 139; allow one only if it must stay reachable.
    sudo ufw allow 53/tcp   # only if this must stay reachable
    sudo ufw allow 80/tcp   # only if this must stay reachable
    sudo ufw allow 111/tcp   # only if this must stay reachable
    sudo ufw allow 139/tcp   # only if this must stay reachable
3. Refuse everything else coming in, and allow everything going out:
    sudo ufw default deny incoming
    sudo ufw default allow outgoing
4. Turn it on and check the result:
    sudo ufw enable
    sudo ufw status verbose

Logins are examined over the last 24 hours; errors and kernel messages over the time since the last boot. Older history is not looked at. Every check is read-only: LinuxDoctor reads logs, it never rotates, cleans or changes them.

findings.title: System Errors Since Boot
findings.explanation:
5000 error message(s) since the last boot, from 2 source(s). 1 of them are at the alert or emergency level, the most serious the system uses. A source that logs this many errors is failing, restarting in a loop or stuck on something; the table shows what it keeps saying.

The journal holds more error messages than were read; the oldest were left out, so the counts are a minimum.

Noisiest sources:
  Count  Source             Message it repeats most
  4999   kernel             ACPI Error: AE_NOT_FOUND, while evaluating GPE method [_L24] (20251212/evgpe-511)
  1      user@1000.service  hp-systray(qt5)[13273]: error: Unable to find hp-upgrade --notify on PATH.
findings.recommendation:
1. Read the most serious messages first:
    sudo journalctl -b -p crit --no-pager
2. See everything kernel reported, newest last:
    sudo journalctl -b -p err -t kernel --no-pager | tail -40
3. Once the cause is fixed, check that the errors stopped (the count should no longer grow):
    sudo journalctl -b -p err --no-pager | wc -l

findings.title: Journal
findings.explanation:
The journal is stored on disk (/var/log/journal): logs survive a reboot.

The journal takes 4.5 GiB, more than the 4.0 GiB journald allows itself when nothing is configured. A limit was probably removed or raised by hand, so it will keep growing.
findings.recommendation:
1. Shrink the journal now:
    journalctl --disk-usage
    sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=1G
2. Cap it for good, in a drop-in file so the distribution's own file stays untouched:
    sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d
    printf '[Journal]\nSystemMaxUse=1G\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/50-size.conf
    sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
